py-easy-01.syntax:
# General form
#   int(x)            -> int built from a number or string
#   int(s, base=10)   -> parse a string in the given base

# How a float is converted: the fractional part is
# discarded, with no rounding to nearest.
# Compare related tools (positive and negative inputs):
import math
x = 7.8
int(x)          # conversion from float
math.floor(x)   # always toward negative infinity
math.ceil(x)    # always toward positive infinity
round(x)        # nearest int, ties go to even

# Strings
int("42")         # 42
int("ff", 16)     # 255
int("  12  ")     # 12 (whitespace is stripped)
# int("3.5")      # ValueError: strings must be integer literals
# int(None)       # TypeError

# Gotchas
# - int(float('nan')) raises ValueError
# - int(float('inf')) raises OverflowError
# - Compare int(), floor() and ceil() on negative numbers;
#   they differ there, so check which direction each goes.
# - Python ints have unlimited size.
py-easy-01.title: Converting floats to integers with int()

docs.title: Built-in Types: Numeric Types (float, nan, inf)

py-easy-02.syntax:
# General form: float(string) can build special values
#   float('inf'), float('-inf'), float('nan')   (case-insensitive)
#   import math; math.inf, math.nan

# Example: infinity behaves like an ordinary, comparable number
big = float('inf')
print(big > 10**100)          # True
print(big == float('INF'))    # True

# Example: testing for the special 'not a number' value
import math
x = math.nan
print(math.isnan(x))          # the reliable test

# Gotchas (comments only):
# - Python follows IEEE 754 for floats: a 'not a number' value is
#   unordered, so ==, <, >, <=, >= against anything (even itself)
#   follow special rules; only != is treated differently.
# - Do not rely on == to detect it; use math.isnan(x).
# - Identity vs equality: `x is x` compares objects, not values.
# - Containers (list, tuple) check identity first, then ==,
#   so `in` and == on lists can differ from direct comparison.
# - float('abc') raises ValueError, but only for strings that
#   are not valid numbers or special names.
# - Arithmetic with it generally yields another such value.
py-easy-02.title: Special float values and comparison semantics (IEEE 754)

py-easy-03.syntax:
# General form
#   a / b    true division
#   a // b   floor division
#   a % b    remainder (modulo)
#   divmod(a, b) -> (a // b, a % b)

# Examples (different values from the quiz)
print(type(9 / 3))     # check the type of a true-division result
print(9 // 4)          # floor division of two ints -> int
print(9.0 // 4)        # with a float operand -> float
print(-9 // 4)         # floors toward negative infinity, not toward zero
print(divmod(17, 5))   # (3, 2)

# Gotchas
# - In Python 3, the / operator always returns a float for int operands,
#   even when the division is exact. Python 2 behaved differently.
# - // returns int only if both operands are int; otherwise float.
# - Dividing by zero raises ZeroDivisionError for / // and %.
# - Float results can have rounding error: 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3.
# - For exact fractions use fractions.Fraction; for exact decimals use decimal.Decimal.
# - int(x) truncates toward zero; math.floor(x) floors.
py-easy-03.title: Arithmetic division operators and numeric result types

py-easy-04.syntax:
# General form
#   a % b   -> remainder r such that a == (a // b) * b + r
#   Python's // floors (rounds toward negative infinity),
#   so the result of % takes the sign of the divisor b.

# Examples (different values from any quiz)
print(10 % 4)      # 2   (positive operands)
print(10 % -4)     # sign follows divisor b (negative or zero)
print(-10 % 4)     # result is in range 0..3 since b > 0

# Check the identity with divmod
q, r = divmod(-9, 5)
# q == -9 // 5, r == -9 % 5
# (q * 5 + r) == -9

# Gotchas
# - Result is 0 <= r < b when b > 0, and b < r <= 0 when b < 0.
# - Differs from C/Java, where % truncates toward zero
#   and takes the sign of the dividend.
# - math.fmod(a, b) follows the C behavior (floats).
# - x % 0 raises ZeroDivisionError.
# - Works on floats too: 5.5 % 2 -> 1.5
py-easy-04.title: Modulo operator with negative operands

py-easy-05.syntax:
# General form: precedence decides which operator grabs its operands first.
# Highest to lowest (excerpt):
#   (expr)            parentheses
#   x[i], x.attr, f() subscripts, attributes, calls
#   await x
#   **                exponentiation
#   +x, -x, ~x        unary plus, minus, bitwise not
#   *, /, //, %       multiplication family
#   +, -              addition, subtraction

# ** binds tighter than a unary operator on its LEFT:
#   -a ** b   is parsed as   -(a ** b)
# ** accepts a unary operator on its RIGHT side:
#   a ** -b   is parsed as   a ** (-b)

# Example with different values:
print(-3 ** 3)     # grouping is -(3 ** 3)
print((-3) ** 3)   # parentheses change the grouping
print(2 ** -1)     # 0.5, negative exponent gives a float

# ** is right-associative:
print(2 ** 3 ** 2)   # 2 ** (3 ** 2)
print((2 ** 3) ** 2) # explicit left grouping differs

# Gotchas:
# - A numeric literal like 5 has no sign; the minus is a separate unary operator.
# - When unsure, add parentheses to make the intent explicit.
# - Even powers of negative bases can differ in sign depending on grouping.
py-easy-05.title: Operator precedence: unary minus and the power operator

py-easy-06.syntax:
# General form
#   a OP1 b OP2 c ...   where OP is any comparison operator
#   (<, <=, >, >=, ==, !=, is, is not, in, not in)
#
# Chains combine the individual comparisons with 'and':
#   a OP1 b OP2 c   behaves like   (a OP1 b) and (b OP2 c)
# The middle operand b is evaluated only once.
# Evaluation short-circuits: if the first comparison is false,
# the later ones are not evaluated.

# Example 1: range check
age = 30
if 18 <= age < 65:
    print("working age")

# Example 2: mixed operators
x = 5
print(0 < x != 10)        # (0 < x) and (x != 10)

# Gotchas
# - Chains can be longer: a < b < c < d
# - Operators can be mixed, including 'in' and 'is':
#       a == b in items   -> (a == b) and (b in items)
# - The outer ends a and c are never compared directly:
#       5 > 3 < 4 is True, even though 5 > 4 isn't tested
# - Chaining is not the same as grouping with parentheses;
#   (a < b) < c compares a bool/result with c.
py-easy-06.title: Chained comparison operators

py-easy-07.syntax:
# General form:
#   left or right
#   left and right
#   not value
#
# Python evaluates operands for truthiness, but `and`/`or`
# return one of the operand objects, not necessarily a bool.
# They short-circuit: the right side runs only if needed.

# Examples (different values from any quiz):
name = "" or "guest"      # left is falsy -> decision moves to right
port = 8080 or 80          # left is truthy -> decided by left
flag = [] and "x"          # and: falsy left decides the result
ok = 7 and "yes"           # and: truthy left -> right operand is used

# Rules of thumb:
# - `a or b`  : returns a if a is truthy, otherwise b
# - `a and b` : returns a if a is falsy, otherwise b
# - `not x`   : always returns a real bool (True/False)
# - Falsy values: None, False, 0, 0.0, "", [], {}, set(), ()
# - Everything else is truthy by default
# - Common idiom: value = user_input or default_value
# - Short-circuit means the skipped operand is never evaluated
# - Use bool(x) if you need a strict True/False
py-easy-07.title: Boolean operators on non-boolean operands

py-easy-08.syntax:
# General form
#   not <expression>
# 'not' first converts the operand to a truth value (truthiness),
# then returns the opposite as a bool (True or False).

# Examples
not 5            # operand is truthy, so the result is the opposite bool
not ""           # empty string is falsy
not [1, 2]       # non-empty list is truthy

# Falsy values (everything else is truthy):
#   None, False
#   zero of any numeric type: 0, 0.0, 0j
#   empty sequences/collections: '', (), [], {}, set(), range(0)
#   objects whose __bool__ returns False or __len__ returns 0

# Gotchas
# - 'not' always returns a bool, unlike 'and' / 'or',
#   which return one of their operands.
#     0 or "hi"   -> "hi"   (operand, not bool)
# - 'not' has lower precedence than comparisons:
#     not a == b   means   not (a == b)
# - 'not' binds tighter than 'and' / 'or':
#     not x and y  means   (not x) and y
# - bool(x) shows the truth value 'not' works from:
#     bool([])  -> False
# - not not x is a way to coerce x to a bool.
py-easy-08.title: Logical negation operator and truthiness

py-easy-09.syntax:
# Subclass relationship check
#   issubclass(Child, Parent) -> bool
#   isinstance(obj, Parent)   -> True also for instances of subclasses
#
# Equality between numbers compares numeric value, not exact type:
#   a == b   (int, float, complex, and subclasses of int compare by value)

print(issubclass(bool, int))   # check a class relationship
print(2.0 == 2)                # different types, compared by value
print(isinstance(False, int))  # instance of a subclass counts

# Gotchas / variations:
# - type(x) is int checks the exact type; isinstance(x, int) accepts subclasses.
# - A subclass inherits the parent's operators, so arithmetic works on it:
#     class Small(int): pass
#     Small(3) + 4        # int arithmetic, result is a plain int
# - Equal values need equal hashes, so equal numbers act as the same
#   dict key / set member:
#     {1, 1.0}            # one element
# - 'is' tests identity, '==' tests value; do not use 'is' to compare numbers.
# - Use type(x).__mro__ to see the full chain of parent classes.
# - bool cannot be subclassed itself, but int can.
py-easy-09.title: Built-in numeric types, subclassing, and equality

py-easy-10.syntax:
# Equality: a == b   -> calls a.__eq__(b); the class decides the result
# Identity: a is b    -> True only if both names refer to the same object
#                        (cannot be overridden by a class)

# Example: a class that customizes equality
class Anything:
    def __eq__(self, other):
        return True          # custom rule: equal to every value

obj = Anything()
print(obj == 42)       # uses the custom __eq__
print(obj is 42)       # identity check (SyntaxWarning for literals)

# Example: singletons
flag = None
print(flag is None)    # idiomatic test for None
print(flag is not None)

# Notes:
# - None, True, False, Ellipsis, NotImplemented are singletons: only one instance exists.
# - Use `is` / `is not` for singleton checks; use == for value comparison.
# - Libraries like NumPy overload == to work elementwise,
#   so `arr == x` may return an array, not a single bool.
# - If __eq__ is defined without __hash__, instances become unhashable.
# - id(a) == id(b) is equivalent to `a is b`.
# - Don't use `is` for numbers or strings; interning is an implementation detail.
py-easy-10.title: Identity vs equality comparison with singletons

py-easy-11.syntax:
# General form
#   isinstance(obj, classinfo) -> bool
# classinfo may be:
#   - a single class
#   - a tuple of classes (nested tuples allowed)
#   - a union type such as A | B (Python 3.10+)

# Example 1: a single class
name = "abc"
isinstance(name, str)            # True

# Example 2: several allowed types
value = [1, 2]
isinstance(value, (list, tuple))      # True if either type matches
isinstance(value, list | tuple)       # same idea, 3.10+ union syntax

# Gotchas
# - isinstance takes exactly two arguments; extra classes are not
#   passed as additional parameters.
# - Only a tuple (or a | union) groups types; a list is not accepted
#   and raises TypeError.
# - Subclasses count: isinstance(True, int) is True because bool
#   subclasses int.
# - Use type(obj) is T for an exact-type check without subclasses.
# - issubclass(cls, classinfo) works the same way, but on classes.
py-easy-11.title: Type checks with isinstance and multiple classes

docs.title: Data model: objects, values and types

py-easy-12.syntax:
# General form of item assignment:
#   sequence[index] = new_value
# It calls the object's __setitem__ method, so it only works
# on types that define it (mutable types).

# Example with a mutable type (dict-like and list-like objects):
scores = [10, 20, 30]
scores[1] = 99          # changes the object in place
scores[-1] = 0          # negative indexes work too
scores[0:2] = [7, 8, 9] # slice assignment can change length

# Example with an immutable type:
point = (4, 5)
# Immutable sequences (tuple, str, bytes) have no __setitem__,
# so trying to assign to an index raises a TypeError.

# Common variations and gotchas:
# - Mutable: list, dict, set, bytearray
# - Immutable: tuple, str, bytes, frozenset, int
# - To "change" an immutable value, build a new one:
#     point = (9,) + point[1:]
# - A tuple can hold a mutable item, and that inner item can be changed:
#     box = ([1, 2], 3)
#     box[0].append(4)   # the inner list changes, the tuple's slots do not
# - Out-of-range index assignment on a list raises IndexError.
# - Check support with hasattr(obj, '__setitem__').
py-easy-12.title: Mutable vs immutable sequence types

docs.title: Data model: objects, values and types

py-easy-13.syntax:
# General form: obj[index] = value
# Item assignment calls obj.__setitem__(index, value).
# It works only if the type defines __setitem__ (mutable types).

# Mutable: list, bytearray, dict
nums = [10, 20, 30]
nums[1] = 99            # item assigned in place

buf = bytearray(b'abc')
buf[0] = 65             # bytearray items are ints

# Immutable: str, tuple, bytes, frozenset
point = (1, 2)
# point[0] = 5          # raises TypeError (no item assignment)

# Building a changed copy of an immutable value:
word = 'python'
new_word = 'P' + word[1:]      # concatenation + slicing
new_word2 = word.replace('p', 'P', 1)
chars = list(word)             # convert to a mutable list
chars[0] = 'P'
joined = ''.join(chars)        # convert back to str

# Gotchas:
# - Rebinding a name (word = 'x') is not mutating the object.
# - String methods return new strings; they never modify the original.
# - A tuple holding a list can have that list's contents changed,
#   but the tuple's own slots cannot be reassigned.
# - Slice assignment (obj[a:b] = ...) also needs a mutable type.
py-easy-13.title: Mutable vs. immutable sequence types and item assignment

py-easy-14.syntax:
# General form: seq[start:stop] or seq[start:stop:step]
# start is included, stop is excluded (half-open range)
# Indexing starts at 0; result is a NEW sequence of the same type

letters = ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e', 'f']
letters[2:5]    # items at index 2, 3, 4
letters[0:2]    # first two items

# Variations and gotchas:
# - Omitted start means 0; omitted stop means len(seq)
#     letters[:3], letters[3:], letters[:] (shallow copy)
# - Negative indexes count from the end: letters[-2:]
# - Out-of-range bounds are clipped, no IndexError
#     letters[4:100] works fine
# - If start >= stop (with positive step), result is empty []
# - step picks every nth item: letters[::2]; step -1 reverses
# - Works on str, tuple, list, range, bytes
# - Number of items returned = stop - start (when in range)
# - slice() objects: letters[slice(1, 4)] is equivalent
py-easy-14.title: Sequence slicing with start:stop

docs.title: Sequence types: indexing and sequence operations

py-easy-15.syntax:
# General form
#   seq[i]
# Non-negative i counts from the left, starting at 0.
# Negative i counts from the right: seq[-k] is seq[len(seq) - k].

# Examples (different values from the question)
word = 'garden'
word[0]    # first character
word[-1]   # last character (-1 is the final position)
word[-3]   # counts back three from the end

nums = [10, 20, 30, 40]
nums[-1]   # works the same for lists and tuples

# Gotchas
# - Valid range is -len(seq) to len(seq)-1; outside it raises IndexError.
# - There is no -0: seq[-0] is seq[0].
# - Strings are immutable: word[-1] = 'x' raises TypeError.
# - Indexing returns a single item (a 1-char str for strings);
#   slicing seq[a:b] returns a sequence and never raises IndexError.
py-easy-15.title: Sequence indexing with negative indices

py-easy-16.syntax:
# General forms
#   seq[start:stop]        # items from start up to (not including) stop
#   seq[start:stop:step]  # optional step
#   seq[i]                # single index lookup

letters = ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e']

# Slicing example
print(letters[1:3])    # ['b', 'c']
print(letters[:2])     # ['a', 'b']
print(letters[::2])    # ['a', 'c', 'e']

# Single index example
print(letters[4])      # 'e'
# letters[9] would raise IndexError: list index out of range

# Gotchas / variations
# - A single index must be within range, otherwise IndexError.
# - Slice bounds are not checked the same way: start and stop are
#   clipped to the sequence length (see the language reference).
# - A slice always produces a new object of the same kind (a list
#   for a list), possibly empty.
# - Negative values count from the end: letters[-2:] -> ['d', 'e']
# - slice(start, stop, step) builds a slice object explicitly.
# - Slicing makes a shallow copy: letters[:] copies the list.
# - A step of 0 raises ValueError.
py-easy-16.title: Sequence slicing and index bounds

py-easy-17.syntax:
# General form: sequence[start:stop:step]
#   start: first index (default depends on step sign)
#   stop:  index to stop BEFORE (exclusive)
#   step:  stride between picked items (default 1)

letters = list("abcdefghij")   # 10 items, indices 0..9
letters[2:8:2]    # start at 2, stop before 8, every 2nd item
letters[1::4]     # from index 1 to the end, every 4th item
letters[::-1]     # negative step walks backwards (reversed copy)

# Notes and gotchas:
# - Omitted start/stop mean "from the beginning/to the end"
#   (reversed when step is negative).
# - The first picked item is at start; then start+step, start+2*step, ...
# - stop is never included.
# - step cannot be 0 (raises ValueError).
# - Out-of-range bounds are clipped, no IndexError for slices.
# - A slice returns a new object of the same kind (list -> list,
#   str -> str, tuple -> tuple).
# - range(n) is a sequence: list(range(n)) gives [0, 1, ..., n-1].
# - slice(start, stop, step) builds a reusable slice object.
py-easy-17.title: Extended slicing with a step

docs.title: copy: shallow and deep copy operations

py-easy-18.syntax:
# General form
#   seq * n        # repeat the elements of seq n times
#   n * seq        # same thing
# Repetition copies REFERENCES to the elements, not the objects themselves.

# Example 1: immutable elements are harmless
names = ['x'] * 3          # three references to the same str; fine, since str can't change

# Example 2: mutable elements are shared
grid = [{}] * 2            # one dict object, referenced twice
print(grid[0] is grid[1])  # identity check: shows whether both slots hold the same object

# Checking sharing
#   a is b          -> True if both names/slots refer to the same object
#   id(a) == id(b)  -> same idea

# Building independent mutable elements
#   [[] for _ in range(n)]        # list comprehension runs the expression each time
#   [dict() for _ in range(n)]    # new object per iteration
#   [list(row) for row in src]    # shallow copy of each inner list

# Gotchas
#   - Applies to list, tuple, str, bytes, etc. (all sequences)
#   - Nested mutable items are shared, not copied
#   - copy.deepcopy(obj) duplicates nested objects recursively
#   - Mutating a shared object is visible through every reference;
#     rebinding a slot (s[i] = new_obj) affects only that slot
py-easy-18.title: Sequence repetition and object references in lists

py-easy-19.syntax:
# General form
#   sequence * n     or     n * sequence
# n must be an integer (int); the result is a new sequence of the same type
# containing the items of the original repeated n times.

# Examples with other values
row = [0] * 4          # a list built from repeated items
dashes = 'x-' * 2      # strings work the same way
pair = (1, 2) * 2      # tuples too

# Variations and gotchas
# - Operand order doesn't matter: 3 * 'ab' is the same kind of expression as 'ab' * 3.
# - n <= 0 gives an empty sequence of the same type ('' , [] , ()).
# - n must be an integer: a float such as 2.0 raises TypeError.
# - No separator is inserted between the copies; the items are joined directly.
# - Lists repeat references, not copies of the items:
#     grid = [[0]] * 3   # three references to the SAME inner list
#     grid[0].append(1)  # appears in every row
# - Don't confuse with str * str, which is not defined and raises TypeError.
# - Does not split or convert the string into a list; the type is preserved.
py-easy-19.title: Sequence repetition with the * operator

py-easy-20.syntax:
# General form
#   seq_a + seq_b      -> new sequence built from both operands
#   seq * n            -> sequence repeated n times
#
# Examples (different values from the quiz)
letters = ['a', 'b'] + ['c']
# a new list is created; the operands are not modified
word = "py" + "thon"          # strings concatenate the same way
pair = (1,) + (2, 3)          # tuples too
pad = [0] * 3                 # repetition with *

# Variations and gotchas
# - Both operands must be the same sequence type.
#   list + tuple raises TypeError; convert first: list(t) + lst
# - + builds a new object each time, so repeated + in a loop is slow;
#   prefer list.extend(), += , or ''.join(...) for strings.
# - lst += other modifies lst in place (accepts any iterable),
#   while lst = lst + other makes a new list.
# - Nesting is different from joining: [lst_a, lst_b] makes a list of lists,
#   whereas + joins the elements into one flat list.
# - [x] * n repeats references to the same object (watch out for nested lists).
# - Numbers add arithmetically: 2 + 3 -> 5; + on sequences never adds elements.
py-easy-20.title: Sequence operators on built-in types

docs.title: Common Sequence Operations / Mutable Sequence Types

py-easy-21.syntax:
# General forms
#   seq.append(obj)       # adds obj as ONE new last element
#   seq.extend(iterable)  # adds EACH item of iterable, in order
#
# Example with different values
box = ['a']
box.append('b')          # box -> ['a', 'b']
box.extend(['c', 'd'])   # each item added separately

items = [10]
items.append((20, 30))   # a tuple stays together as one element
items.extend((40, 50))   # tuple is iterated; elements added one by one

# Variations and gotchas
# - Both modify the list in place and return None (don't write x = x.append(1)).
# - append takes exactly one argument, whatever its type.
# - extend accepts any iterable: list, tuple, set, generator, range, dict (keys).
# - extend with a string adds each character: s = []; s.extend('hi') -> ['h', 'i']
# - seq += iterable behaves like extend.
# - seq + other builds a NEW list; it does not modify seq.
# - Appending a list creates nesting; len grows by 1 per append call,
#   but by len(iterable) per extend call.
py-easy-21.title: Adding items to a list: single item vs. iterable

py-easy-22.syntax:
# General form
# list.insert(index, item)   -> returns None, modifies the list in place
# list.append(item)         -> adds one item at the end
# list.extend(iterable)     -> adds each element of iterable at the end

# Example with different values
nums = [10, 20, 30]
nums.insert(0, 5)       # a method call on the list itself
print(nums)             # shows the list after the call

# Related variations
# nums[1] = 99          # item assignment: overwrites the element at that index
# nums[1:1] = [7, 8]    # slice assignment: splices several items in

# Gotchas
# - insert() returns None, so don't write: nums = nums.insert(0, 5)
# - Items at and after the index shift one position to the right.
# - An index larger than len(list) is not an error; it goes at the end.
# - A negative index counts from the end: insert(-1, x) goes before the last item.
# - insert(len(lst), x) behaves like append(x).
# - Inserting near the front is O(n); append is amortized O(1).
py-easy-22.title: List methods for adding items by position

docs.title: Common Sequence Operations / Mutable Sequence Types

py-easy-23.syntax:
# General forms
#   seq.remove(x)    -> searches by value, returns None
#   seq.pop()        -> removes item at the end, returns it
#   seq.pop(i)       -> removes item at position i, returns it
#   del seq[i]       -> removes by position, returns nothing

letters = ['a', 'b', 'c', 'b', 'd']

letters.remove('c')      # argument is a VALUE to look for
print(letters)           # ['a', 'b', 'b', 'd']

got = letters.pop(0)     # argument is an INDEX (position)
print(got)               # 'a'  (the removed item is returned)

last = letters.pop()     # no argument: uses the last position

# Gotchas
# - remove(x) affects only the FIRST matching element;
#   later duplicates stay in the list.
# - remove(x) raises ValueError if x is not in the list.
# - pop(i) raises IndexError if the list is empty
#   or i is out of range.
# - Negative indexes work with pop: pop(-2).
# - To drop all matches, build a new list:
#   nums = [n for n in nums if n != 3]
# - Avoid removing from a list while looping over it.
py-easy-23.title: Removing items from a Python list

docs.title: Common Sequence Operations: mutable sequence types

py-easy-24.syntax:
# General form
#   seq.pop()        -> removes and returns an item (default index argument)
#   seq.pop(i)       -> removes and returns the item at index i
#
# Example
letters = ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd']
x = letters.pop(1)      # x is the item at index 1
print(x, letters)       # the list is modified in place

nums = [10, 20, 30]
y = nums.pop(0)         # explicit index

# Notes and gotchas
# - The signature is list.pop([i]); the index defaults to a fixed position.
#   Check the docs to see which one the default is.
# - Negative indexes count from the end: pop(-2).
# - pop() mutates the list and returns the removed value.
# - Empty list, or index out of range, raises IndexError.
# - Cost depends on position: removing near the front shifts
#   remaining items, so it is slower for long lists.
# - Compare: remove(value) deletes by value and returns None;
#   del lst[i] deletes by index without returning.
# - dict.pop(key[, default]) and set.pop() behave differently.
py-easy-24.title: list.pop() method

py-easy-25.syntax:
# General form
del target_list
#   del seq[index]        -> removes the item at that position
#   del seq[start:stop]   -> removes a slice of items
#   del name              -> unbinds a variable name
#   del d[key]            -> removes a key from a dict

# Example 1: a list of numbers
nums = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
del nums[0]          # statement, returns nothing
# later items shift left, so indexes change afterward

# Example 2: slice and dict
letters = list('uvwxyz')
del letters[1:3]     # stop index is excluded
del letters[::2]     # extended slices work too
ages = {'amy': 31, 'raj': 28}
del ages['amy']

# Gotchas
# - del is a statement, not a function or expression:
#     x = del nums[0]   # SyntaxError
# - Out-of-range index raises IndexError; missing key raises KeyError.
# - Negative indexes count from the end: del nums[-1]
# - Deleting while looping over the same list skips items.
# - Related alternatives: list.pop(i) returns the removed item,
#   list.remove(value) removes the first match by value,
#   list.clear() empties the list but keeps the object.
# - Assigning None to an element (nums[0] = None) is different:
#   it keeps the slot and the length does not change.
py-easy-25.title: The del statement on sequence items and slices

py-easy-26.syntax:
# General forms
#   seq.method_name(...)      -> method called on an object
#   builtin_name(iterable)    -> function called with an argument
#
# Both sorting tools accept key= and reverse= keyword arguments:
#   list.sort(*, key=None, reverse=False)
#   sorted(iterable, /, *, key=None, reverse=False)

# Example 1: the method form on a list named nums
nums = [9, 4, 7]
r1 = nums.sort(reverse=True)
print(nums)   # inspect the list afterwards
print(r1)     # inspect what the call itself evaluated to

# Example 2: the function form on a tuple named words
words = ("pear", "fig", "apple")
r2 = sorted(words, key=len)
print(words)  # is the original touched?
print(r2)     # what type is the result?

# Gotchas / variations
# - Mutating methods in Python conventionally return None
#   (e.g. list.append, list.reverse) to signal in-place change.
#   So `x = y.sort()` is a common bug.
# - sort() exists only on list; sorted() works on any iterable
#   (tuple, set, dict keys, generator, str) and always returns a list.
# - Sorting is stable: equal keys keep their original order.
# - key= takes a one-argument function, called once per element.
# - Mixed incomparable types (int vs str) raise TypeError.
py-easy-26.title: Sorting lists: list method vs built-in function

py-easy-27.syntax:
# General form
# sorted(iterable, /, *, key=None, reverse=False) -> new list
#   - returns a NEW list; the original is not modified
#   - key and reverse are keyword-only (must be passed by name)
#   - works on any iterable (list, tuple, str, dict keys, set...)

# Example 1: key function
words = ['pear', 'fig', 'banana']
by_len = sorted(words, key=len)

# Example 2: combining key with another keyword
nums = [4, 9, 1]
result = sorted(nums, key=lambda n: n % 3, reverse=False)

# Variations and gotchas:
# - Only the parameters listed in the signature exist; passing an
#   unknown keyword name raises TypeError.
# - Sorting is stable: equal items keep their original order,
#   even when reverse is used.
# - list.sort() is the in-place method with the same key/reverse
#   options; it returns None.
# - Slicing with [::-1] reverses a sequence; that is reversing,
#   not sorting by a rule.
# - reversed(seq) returns an iterator, and there is no builtin
#   named reverse().
# - Mixed types that can't be compared (int vs str) raise TypeError.
py-easy-27.title: sorted() builtin: keyword arguments and ordering

py-easy-28.syntax:
# General form
sorted(iterable, *, key=None, reverse=False)  # returns a NEW list

# key is a callable (any one-argument function, not just a string).
# Each element is passed to key once; the returned values are compared
# to decide the order. The original elements are what end up in the result.

# Example 1: built-in as key
words = ['pear', 'apple', 'plum']
sorted(words, key=str.lower)      # sorts by lowercase form

# Example 2: lambda as key
pairs = [(1, 'b'), (2, 'a')]
sorted(pairs, key=lambda p: p[1]) # sorts by second item

# Variations and gotchas
# - reverse=True flips the order (equal items keep original order).
# - Sorting is stable: items with equal keys keep their input order.
# - Pass the function itself (key=len), do not call it (key=len() is wrong).
# - key values must be comparable with each other.
# - list.sort(key=...) works the same but sorts in place and returns None.
# - Without key, items are compared directly (strings alphabetically).
py-easy-28.title: sorted() with a key function

py-easy-29.syntax:
# General form
#   max(iterable, *, key=None, default=...)
#   min(iterable, *, key=None, default=...)
# key is a one-argument function called once per item;
# items are compared by the value key returns, but the
# original item is what gets returned.

words = ['pear', 'fig', 'banana', 'kiwi']
min(words, key=len)                  # compares 3, 4, 4, 6 lengths
max(words, key=lambda w: w[-1])      # compare by last letter

# Other forms
#   max(1, 5, 3)                     # several positional args
#   max([], default=0)               # default avoids ValueError on empty
#   max(d, key=d.get)                # dict key with the largest value
#   max(people, key=lambda p: p.age) # objects by attribute

# Gotchas
# - Result is an element of the iterable, not the key value.
# - Ties: the FIRST item with the best key is returned.
# - Without key, items are compared directly (str by alphabet).
# - Empty iterable without default raises ValueError.
# - key must be passed by keyword.
# - sorted(), list.sort() accept key= the same way.
py-easy-29.title: The key= argument of max() and min()

py-easy-30.syntax:
# General form
# sum(iterable, /, start=0)
#   Begins with `start`, then adds each item from the iterable, left to right.
#   Returns the running total after the last item.

# Example 1: default start
sum([4, 5])            # start is 0 by default

# Example 2: explicit start value
sum([1.5, 2.5], 100)   # the total begins at 100 and the items are added to it

# Variations and gotchas
# - An empty iterable returns start unchanged: sum([], 7)
# - start is positional-or-keyword in modern Python: sum(nums, start=5)
# - start is NOT another item to add to the list; it is the initial accumulator
# - Works with any iterable of numbers: tuples, sets, generators, range()
# - Non-numeric items raise TypeError: sum(["a", "b"]) fails because start=0 is an int
# - For lists, tuples, etc. pass a matching start, e.g. sum([[1], [2]], [])
#   (but this is slow; prefer itertools.chain)
# - Strings are rejected explicitly; use "".join(...)
# - For exact float summation use math.fsum()
py-easy-30.title: The built-in sum() function and its start argument

py-easy-31.syntax:
# General form
#   len(obj) -> int
# Calls obj.__len__(); works for any object that defines it.
# Objects without __len__ raise TypeError.

# Examples
len("hello")            # sequence: number of characters
len(range(2, 20, 3))     # range is also supported
len(b"ab")               # bytes too

class Bag:
    def __init__(self, items):
        self.items = items
    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.items)

len(Bag([1, 2, 3]))      # uses the custom __len__

# Variations and gotchas
# - Sequences (str, bytes, list, tuple, range) and
#   collections (dict, frozenset, set) are the usual built-in
#   types to check against the docs.
# - Iterators and generators have no length:
#   len(x for x in [1]) -> TypeError
# - Numbers and None have no length:
#   len(42) -> TypeError: object of type 'int' has no len()
# - __len__ must return an int >= 0, else ValueError/TypeError.
# - len(obj) == 0 also makes an object falsy if no __bool__.
# - Check support with: hasattr(obj, "__len__")
py-easy-31.title: Built-in len() and the container protocol

py-easy-32.syntax:
# General form
#   range(stop)
#   range(start, stop)
#   range(start, stop, step)
# start defaults to 0, step defaults to 1.
# The stop value is EXCLUSIVE: it is never produced.

# Examples (different values from any quiz)
r = range(2, 9, 3)
print(list(r))        # [2, 5, 8]
print(len(range(10))) # count of items = stop - start for step 1

for i in range(3):    # i takes the values 0, 1, 2
    pass

# Variations and gotchas
# - range(n) yields n items when start is 0 and step is 1.
# - Negative step counts down: list(range(6, 0, -2)) -> [6, 4, 2]
# - If start >= stop with a positive step, the range is empty: list(range(4, 4)) -> []
# - step=0 raises ValueError.
# - range is a lazy, immutable sequence, not a list; it supports len(), indexing,
#   slicing, and `in`, and uses little memory regardless of size.
# - list(iterable) builds a new list by consuming every item.
# - Behavior is the same on every platform and Python 3 implementation.
py-easy-32.title: The range() sequence type and converting it to a list

py-easy-33.syntax:
# General form
# range(stop)
# range(start, stop)
# range(start, stop, step)
#   start defaults to 0, step defaults to 1
#   stop is EXCLUSIVE: the sequence never includes it
#   step must not be 0 (raises ValueError)

# Example 1: positive step
list(range(3, 15, 4))     # starts at 3, adds 4 while value < 15

# Example 2: negative step
for n in range(20, 5, -5):
    print(n)              # counts down while value > stop

# Gotchas
# - range is a lazy sequence, not a list; wrap in list() to see values
# - With a positive step, items are generated while value < stop;
#   with a negative step, while value > stop
# - If start already fails that test, the result is empty:
#   list(range(1, 5, -1)) -> []
# - Arguments must be integers (no floats)
# - len(r), r[i], r[::-1], and `x in r` all work on a range
# - To include the stop value, adjust it by one step's direction
py-easy-33.title: range() with start, stop, and step

py-easy-34.syntax:
# General form
# enumerate(iterable, start=0)
# Returns a lazy iterator of (index, item) tuples.
# The counter begins at `start`; the items are not changed or skipped.

# Example 1: loop with a counter
for n, color in enumerate(['red', 'green', 'blue']):
    print(n, color)

# Example 2: custom starting number, materialized into a list
list(enumerate('xyz', start=10))

# Variations and gotchas
# - start can be positional: enumerate(items, 5)
# - The counter increases by 1 for each item, whatever start is.
# - start only affects the number; it does not slice the iterable.
# - Each pair is (index, item), index first.
# - The result is an iterator: wrap in list() or tuple() to see it all,
#   and it can be consumed only once.
# - Works with any iterable (strings, files, generators, dicts).
# - dict(enumerate(seq)) builds an index -> item mapping.
py-easy-34.title: Built-in enumerate() and its start parameter

py-easy-35.syntax:
# General form
# zip(*iterables, strict=False) -> iterator of tuples
#   Each tuple holds one item from each iterable, by position.

# Example with equal-length inputs
names = ['x', 'y', 'z']
vals = [10, 20, 30]
print(list(zip(names, vals)))   # [('x', 10), ('y', 20), ('z', 30)]

# Example with three iterables
print(list(zip('ab', [1, 2], (True, False))))

# Gotchas and variations
# - zip returns a lazy iterator, so wrap in list() to see all items.
# - It can be consumed only once.
# - Unequal lengths: the default behavior is decided by the SHORTEST
#   input; check the docs for what happens to leftover items.
# - strict=True (Python 3.10+) raises ValueError if lengths differ.
# - To pad a shorter input with a fill value, use
#   itertools.zip_longest(a, b, fillvalue=...).
# - zip(*pairs) unpacks pairs back into separate sequences.
# - zip() with no arguments yields nothing.
# - dict(zip(keys, values)) builds a dict from two sequences.
py-easy-35.title: Combining iterables with zip() and unequal lengths

py-easy-36.syntax:
# General form:
#   it = builtin_func(iterable)      # many built-ins return an iterator, not a list
#   next(it)                         # get one item at a time
#   list(it)                         # materialize all items into a list

# Example: map returns a lazy iterator
m = map(str.upper, ['a', 'b', 'c'])
print(type(m))          # <class 'map'>
print(next(m))          # 'A'
print(list(m))          # ['B', 'C']  (already consumed 'A')

# Example: materialize before indexing
z = list(zip([1, 2], ['x', 'y']))
print(z[0])             # (1, 'x')

# Gotchas:
# - Indexing (obj[i]) needs __getitem__; many iterators don't have it.
# - Iterators are single-use: once consumed, they are empty.
# - Check with: type(obj), iter(obj) is obj (True for iterators).
# - Same family: enumerate, filter, zip, map, reversed.
# - To get a reversed list instead: list(reversed(seq)) or seq[::-1]
# - sorted() is different: it always returns a new list.
py-easy-36.title: Built-in iterator-returning functions and sequence access

py-easy-37.syntax:
# General form
#   all(iterable) -> bool
# Returns a bool: True if every element is truthy (or the iterable is empty),
# otherwise False. It always returns True/False, never an element.
# Short-circuits: stops at the first falsy element.

# Examples
all([4, 5, 6])          # every item truthy
all(x > 0 for x in [3, 8, 1])   # works with generator expressions
all([])                 # empty iterable -> vacuous truth

# Truthiness rules
# Falsy: 0, 0.0, '', [], {}, set(), None, False
# Everything else is truthy (non-zero numbers, non-empty containers)

# Gotchas
# - Result is a bool, not the offending/last element (unlike `and` chains).
# - Argument must be iterable: all(5) raises TypeError.
# - Strings are iterables of characters: all('ab') checks each char.
# - Related: any(iterable) is True if at least one element is truthy;
#   any([]) is False.
py-easy-37.title: Built-in all() and truthiness of iterables

py-easy-38.syntax:
# General form
#   map(function, iterable, *more_iterables)  -> lazy iterator (map object)
#   list(map(...))                            -> materialize the results
#   lambda args: expression                   -> small anonymous function

# Example 1: apply a function to each item
names = ["ann", "bo"]
print(list(map(lambda s: s.upper(), names)))   # applies to each element

# Example 2: several iterables, function takes several args
a = [1, 2]
b = [10, 20]
print(list(map(lambda x, y: x + y, a, b)))     # pairs items by position

# Gotchas
# - map() returns an iterator, not a list; printing it directly shows
#   something like <map object at 0x...>.
# - An iterator can be consumed only once.
# - With multiple iterables, map stops at the shortest one.
# - The function is applied to each element individually; the input
#   sequence is not repeated or reduced to a single value.
# - Equivalent list comprehension: [f(x) for x in items]
# - Pass a named function too: list(map(str, [1, 2]))
py-easy-38.title: map() with lambda and list()

py-easy-39.syntax:
# General form
#   filter(function, iterable) -> lazy iterator
#   Keeps items for which function(item) is truthy.
#   function may be a lambda or a named function.
#   filter returns an iterator (not a list); wrap with list() to see items.

# Example 1: keep words longer than 3 characters
words = ['cat', 'horse', 'ox', 'tiger']
long_words = list(filter(lambda w: len(w) > 3, words))

# Example 2: named predicate
def is_multiple_of_three(n):
    return n % 3 == 0

list(filter(is_multiple_of_three, range(10)))

# Variations and gotchas
# - filter(None, iterable) keeps only truthy items (drops 0, '', None, [] ...).
# - The items themselves are returned unchanged; filter selects, it does not transform.
#   (Use map(f, it) to transform: it yields f(item) for each item.)
# - The result is lazy and can be consumed only once.
# - Equivalent comprehension: [x for x in iterable if function(x)]
# - itertools.filterfalse(f, it) keeps items where f(item) is falsy.
# - lambda args: expression  -> anonymous one-expression function.
# - x % 2 is the remainder after dividing by 2.
py-easy-39.title: filter() with a predicate function

py-easy-40.syntax:
# General form:
#   lambda <parameters>: <single expression>
# - keyword `lambda`, then parameters separated by commas, NO parentheses around them
# - a colon `:` separates parameters from the body
# - the body is one expression; its value is returned automatically (no `return`)

multiply = lambda a, b: a * b
print(multiply(3, 4))          # call it like any function

words = ["pear", "fig", "banana"]
words.sort(key=lambda w: len(w))   # common use: inline key function

# Variations:
#   lambda: 42                    -> no parameters
#   lambda n, step=1: n + step    -> default values allowed
#   lambda *args, **kw: args      -> varargs allowed
#   (lambda s: s.upper())("hi")   -> can be called immediately
#
# Gotchas:
# - Body must be an expression: no statements (assignment, return, if-block, etc.)
# - Use a conditional expression for branching: lambda n: "pos" if n > 0 else "non-pos"
# - No `->` return annotation and no `=` in the lambda header
# - Python 3 does not allow tuple parameters like lambda(a, b): ...
# - For anything longer than one expression, use `def`
py-easy-40.title: Python lambda expressions (anonymous functions)

py-easy-41.syntax:
# General form
# [expression for item in iterable]
# [expression for item in iterable if condition]

# Example: build a new list from another sequence
names = ["ada", "bob", "cy"]
lengths = [len(n) for n in names]   # one element per item, in order

# Example: filter with a condition
big = [n for n in range(10, 15) if n % 2 == 0]

# Variations and gotchas:
# - Square brackets build a list immediately.
#   Parentheses (expr for x in it) make a generator expression instead.
#   Braces {expr for x in it} make a set; {k: v for ...} makes a dict.
# - range(n) yields 0 up to n-1 (stop value is excluded).
# - The expression is evaluated once per item, using that item's value.
# - Conditional value (if/else) goes BEFORE the for:
#     [a if a > 0 else 0 for a in values]
# - Nested loops read left to right, like nested for statements:
#     [(i, j) for i in range(2) for j in range(3)]
# - The loop variable does not leak into the enclosing scope.
py-easy-41.title: List comprehensions

docs.title: Displays for lists, sets and dictionaries (Language Reference)

py-easy-42.syntax:
# General form:
# [expression for item in iterable if condition]
#
# Reads like this loop:
# result = []
# for item in iterable:
#     if condition:
#         result.append(expression)

words = ["apple", "fig", "banana", "kiwi"]
short = [w.upper() for w in words if len(w) <= 4]
# built from only the items where the condition is True

# Variations and gotchas:
# - range(stop) yields 0 up to stop-1 (stop is excluded)
# - the `if` filters items; items failing it are skipped, not replaced
# - x % n is the remainder after dividing x by n; x % n == 0 means
#   x is divisible by n
# - the expression part can transform the item, the condition only
#   decides whether the item is kept
# - several conditions: [x for x in data if x > 2 if x < 8]
# - if/else INSIDE the expression (before `for`) is different:
#   [a if a > 0 else 0 for a in data]   # keeps every item
# - nested loops: [(i, j) for i in A for j in B if i != j]
# - the result is always a new list; the source is unchanged
py-easy-42.title: List comprehensions with a filter condition

py-easy-43.syntax:
# General forms (the delimiters and the element expression decide the type):
#   [ expr for item in iterable ]            -> list comprehension
#   { expr for item in iterable }            -> set comprehension
#   { key: value for item in iterable }      -> dict comprehension
#   ( expr for item in iterable )            -> generator expression (not a tuple)

# Examples with different values:
words = ["a", "bb", "ccc"]
[w.upper() for w in words]        # list of transformed items
{len(w) for w in words}           # set: duplicates collapse, no order guarantee
{w: len(w) for w in words}        # dict: each iteration builds a key: value pair

# Optional filter goes at the end:
{n: n + 1 for n in range(10) if n % 2 == 0}

# Variations and gotchas:
# - The "key: value" colon is what makes a dict; without it, braces make a set.
# - Empty {} is an empty dict, not an empty set (use set()).
# - Duplicate keys: later values overwrite earlier ones.
# - Multiple loops: [a + b for a in xs for b in ys]
# - The loop variable does not leak into the enclosing scope.
# - A tuple needs tuple(...) around a generator expression.
py-easy-43.title: Python comprehensions: brackets and element form

docs.title: Displays for lists, sets and dictionaries

py-easy-44.syntax:
# General forms (the brackets decide the result type):
#   [expr for item in iterable]            -> list
#   {expr for item in iterable}            -> set
#   {key: val for item in iterable}        -> dict
#   (expr for item in iterable)            -> generator (not a tuple)
#   optional filter: ... for item in it if cond

words = ["a", "bb", "cc", "ddd"]

lengths_list = [len(w) for w in words]   # a list built item by item
lengths_set  = {len(w) for w in words}   # a set built item by item
by_word = {w: len(w) for w in words}     # a dict

# Gotchas:
# - A set literal/comprehension holds unique elements only;
#   adding a value already present changes nothing.
# - Sets are unordered: do not rely on display order.
# - {} alone is an empty dict; use set() for an empty set.
# - {k: v for ...} makes a dict, {e for ...} makes a set.
# - Parentheses give a generator expression, not a tuple;
#   use tuple(expr for ...) for a tuple.
# - The loop variable does not leak out of a comprehension.
# - x % n gives the remainder after division by n.
py-easy-44.title: Comprehensions with braces

py-easy-45.syntax:
# General form: apply one subscript per level, left to right
#   container[index_or_key][index_or_key]...
#   list  -> integer position (0-based, negative counts from the end)
#   dict  -> key (must match exactly, strings need quotes)

# Example: a list of dicts
items = [{'sku': 'A1', 'qty': 3}, {'sku': 'B2', 'qty': 7}]
first = items[0]          # the whole dict at position 0
items[0]['sku']           # first pick the list element, then the key
items[-1]['qty']          # last element, then key

# Example: a dict holding a list
team = {'langs': ['go', 'rust', 'c']}
team['langs'][2]          # key first, then position

# Gotchas:
# - Read the expression from left to right; each step must match
#   the type of what the previous step returned.
# - Dict keys are written as values: d['k'] uses a string, d[k] looks up a variable named k.
# - Dict entries are not attributes: d.key raises AttributeError (dicts have no such attribute).
# - A list needs an int index; a str index raises TypeError.
# - Missing key -> KeyError; position out of range -> IndexError.
# - d.get('k') returns None instead of raising KeyError.
py-easy-45.title: Indexing nested lists and dictionaries

py-easy-46.syntax:
# General form
for item in iterable:
    ...            # loop body
    if condition:
        break      # optional early exit
else:
    ...            # extra block attached to the loop

# Example 1: searching a list
names = ["ann", "bob", "cy"]
for n in names:
    if n.startswith("z"):
        print("found z-name")
        break
else:
    print("no z-name in list")

# Example 2: while loop has the same form
i = 0
while i < 3:
    i += 1
else:
    print("while finished, i =", i)

# Notes / gotchas
# - The else belongs to the loop, not to an if inside it.
# - Think of it as "no break happened".
# - Check what each way of leaving the loop does to the else block:
#   break, return, raise, continue, and the iterable running out.
# - An empty iterable (or a false while condition at the start)
#   still lets the loop end normally; consider what that means for else.
# - Common use: search loops, replacing a "found" flag variable.
py-easy-46.title: Loop else clauses (for/while ... else)

py-easy-47.syntax:
# General form (inside for or while body):
#   for item in iterable:
#       ...
#       break      # loop-control statement
#       continue   # loop-control statement
#   else:          # optional, runs if loop was not ended by break
#       ...

# Example 1: scanning for a value
for name in ["ann", "bo", "cy"]:
    if name == "bo":
        print("found")
        break
else:
    print("not found")

# Example 2: filtering inside a loop
total = 0
for n in range(6):
    if n % 2 == 0:
        continue
    total += n

# Notes and gotchas:
# - Both statements work in for loops AND while loops.
# - Both affect only the innermost enclosing loop.
# - Using either outside a loop is a SyntaxError.
# - In a while loop, continue jumps back to re-check the condition;
#   make sure the counter is updated before continue, or it may loop forever.
# - In a for loop, continue moves on to the next item from the iterator.
# - The loop's else block is skipped when break runs.
# - In try/finally, the finally clause still runs before leaving or moving on.
py-easy-47.title: Loop control statements: break, continue, and loop else

py-easy-49.syntax:
# General form: targets on the left, values on the right
#   target1, target2, ... = value1, value2, ...
# The right side is built first (a tuple), then its items are
# assigned to the targets left to right, by position.

x, y, z = 10, 20, 30      # three targets, three values
print(x, y, z)

# Works with any iterable on the right side
first, second = "hi"      # string of length 2
m, n = [7, 8]             # list of length 2

# Swapping uses the same rule: right side is evaluated fully first
p, q = 5, 6
p, q = q, p

# Gotchas (as comments):
# - Number of targets must match number of values, otherwise
#   ValueError (too many / not enough values to unpack).
# - Parentheses on either side are optional: (u, v) = (1, 2)
# - A starred target collects the rest into a list:
#     head, *rest = [1, 2, 3, 4]
# - Each name is bound to one item, not to the whole tuple.
# - Use _ by convention for values you want to ignore.
py-easy-49.title: Tuple packing and unpacking in assignment

py-easy-50.syntax:
# General form: one starred target collects the "leftover" items
#   first, *middle, last = iterable
#   *head, tail = iterable
#   head, *tail = iterable
#
# Rules:
# - At most one starred target per assignment.
# - Non-starred targets each take exactly one item (matched from the ends).
# - The starred target always becomes a list (never a tuple or the original type).
# - If nothing is left over, the starred target is an empty list.
# - The iterable must have at least as many items as non-starred targets,
#   otherwise ValueError.

# Example 1
x, *y, z = (10, 20, 30, 40)
# x gets the first item, z gets the last, y is a list of what is between

# Example 2: works with any iterable, including strings and ranges
first, *rest = "hey"
# first is a str of one char; rest is a list of the remaining chars

# Variations
# *a, b = [7]       -> a is [] (empty list), b is 7
# a, b, *c = [1]    -> ValueError (not enough values)
# *a, *b = [1, 2]   -> SyntaxError (two starred targets)
# _, *middle, _ = data   # common idiom to ignore the ends

# Also used in for loops:
# for head, *tail in [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5]]:
#     ...
py-easy-50.title: Starred assignment (extended iterable unpacking)

py-easy-51.syntax:
# General form: the right side is evaluated fully first, then
# its items are assigned to the targets on the left, left to right.
#   target1, target2, ... = expr1, expr2, ...

# Example 1: reorder values of two names
x, y, z = 1, 2, 3
z, x = x, z          # right side (x, z) is built BEFORE any name is rebound

# Example 2: unpack any iterable
first, second = [10, 20]
head, *rest = "abc"  # starred target collects the remainder as a list

# Variations and gotchas:
# - Number of targets must match the number of values (unless one is starred),
#   otherwise ValueError.
# - Sequential assignments (p = q; q = p) are separate statements: the first
#   one overwrites a value the second one still needs.
#   A helper variable fixes that, but takes extra lines.
# - Works with indexes too: items[0], items[1] = items[1], items[0]
# - Parentheses are optional: (m, n) = (n, m) is the same.
# - Python has no built-in swap() function; a user-defined function cannot
#   rebind the caller's local names.
py-easy-51.title: Tuple packing and unpacking in assignment

py-easy-54.syntax:
# General form: one value, several targets
#   x = y = z = <expression>
# The expression is evaluated ONCE; the resulting object is
# bound to each target from left to right.

# Example with an immutable value
p = q = 7
print(p is q)          # names refer to the same int object

# Example with a different mutable value
u = v = {"k": 1}
u["j"] = 2             # mutates the one shared dict
print(v)               # visible through every name bound to it

# Checking sharing
#   x is y             -> True if both names refer to the same object
#   id(x) == id(y)     -> same idea

# Gotchas
# - Names are references, not copies; mutating via one name
#   is seen through all names bound to the same object.
# - Rebinding (x = new_value) only changes that one name.
# - To get independent objects, evaluate separately:
#       s = []; t = []
#       s, t = [], []
#   or copy: t = s.copy()  /  copy.deepcopy(s) for nested data
# - Similar trap: [[]] * 3 repeats a reference to one inner list.
py-easy-54.title: Chained assignment and object identity

py-easy-55.syntax:
# General form
#   dict.keys(), dict.values(), dict.items()  -> "dictionary view objects"
#
# Example with different names/values
stock = {"pear": 3, "fig": 7}
v = stock.values()
for name, qty in stock.items():   # unpack each pair
    print(name, qty)

# Things to check about any view object:
#   - type(view) is a special class (dict_items, dict_keys, dict_values),
#     not list, tuple, or generator
#   - Can it be iterated more than once? Is len() supported?
#   - Does it reflect later changes to the dict, or not?
#   - Does `in` work on it directly?
#
# Experiment yourself:
#   w = stock.keys()
#   stock["plum"] = 1
#   print(len(w), list(w))   # observe what happens
#
# Gotchas:
#   - Changing dict size while iterating a view raises RuntimeError
#   - list(view) makes an independent copy
#   - keys() and items() views support set-like operations (&, |, -, ^)
#   - values() views do not support set operations
#   - Views are iterable in dict insertion order (Python 3.7+)
#   - Views are not indexable: view[0] raises TypeError
py-easy-55.title: Dictionary view objects

py-easy-56.syntax:
# General forms
#   d[key]            -> value, or raises KeyError if key is missing
#   d.get(key)        -> value, or None if key is missing
#   d.get(key, dflt)  -> value, or dflt if key is missing

# Examples
stock = {'apple': 5, 'pear': 2}
stock.get('apple', 99)    # key present: stored value is returned
stock.get('plum')         # one-argument form: falls back to None
len(stock.get('kiwi', []))  # default can be any object

# Gotchas
# - .get() never raises KeyError and never modifies the dict.
# - The default is evaluated every call, even if the key exists,
#   so avoid expensive expressions as the default.
# - If the key exists with value None, .get(key, dflt) returns None,
#   not dflt (the default only applies to missing keys).
# - To insert a missing key as well, use d.setdefault(key, dflt).
# - Lookup uses the key itself, never the default, as the result of a miss.
# - Keys must be hashable and match by equality: 1 and 1.0 are the same key.
py-easy-56.title: Dict lookup with a fallback value

py-easy-57.syntax:
# General form
#   value = mapping.setdefault(key, default)
#
# Rule: look up key.
#   - if key exists: return its current value, mapping unchanged
#   - if key is missing: insert key with default, then return default
# The return value is the object stored in the dict (not a copy).
# default is optional and defaults to None.

# Example 1: scalar default
stock = {'apple': 3}
n = stock.setdefault('apple', 0)   # key present -> existing value returned
m = stock.setdefault('pear', 5)    # key absent  -> 5 is stored and returned

# Example 2: grouping with a mutable default
groups = {}
for word in ['ant', 'bee', 'axe']:
    groups.setdefault(word[0], []).append(word)
# Returned list is the same object held by the dict, so mutating it
# through the return value changes the dict's contents.

# Gotchas
# - The default expression is evaluated every call, even if key exists
#   (a new [] is built and discarded when not needed).
# - Only one lookup/insert step; no KeyError is raised for missing keys.
# - Alternative: collections.defaultdict(list) avoids repeating the default.
# - Compare: d.get(key, default) returns default but does NOT insert it.
py-easy-57.title: dict.setdefault() method

py-easy-58.syntax:
# General form
#   element in container      -> bool
#   element not in container  -> bool
#
# For a dict, the container is searched according to the dict's own
# iteration/lookup rules (hash lookup), the same thing you get
# when you iterate over the dict directly.

stock = {'apple': 3, 'pear': 0}

# Example: test a name against the dict
print('pear' in stock)

# Example: testing the other parts explicitly
print(3 in stock.values())      # search the values (linear scan)
print(('apple', 3) in stock.items())  # search key/value pairs

# Variations and gotchas
# - list(stock) and `for k in stock` yield the same things that
#   `in` checks against.
# - Key lookup is O(1) on average; .values() search is O(n).
# - Keys must be hashable; `[1] in stock` raises TypeError.
# - `not in` is the negated form: 'kiwi' not in stock
# - .keys() gives a set-like view: 'apple' in stock.keys()
# - Use stock.get(key) or `in` to avoid KeyError from stock[key].
# - Equal keys match: 1, 1.0 and True hash and compare equal.
py-easy-58.title: Membership testing with the in operator on mappings

py-easy-59.syntax:
# General form
#   needle in haystack        -> bool
#   needle not in haystack    -> bool (the negation)

# For str haystacks, `in` tests for a contiguous substring
# (the needle must itself be a str).
print('ab' in 'crabs')         # substring test example
print('xyz' not in 'crabs')    # negated form

# For lists, tuples, sets, dicts: tests for an element
# (for dict, tests keys).
fruits = ['apple', 'pear']
print('pear' in fruits)        # element test
print('ear' in fruits)         # compares against whole elements, not parts

# Variations and gotchas
# - Matching is case-sensitive: 'A' in 'abc' differs from 'a' in 'abc'.
# - Order and adjacency matter for strings: characters must appear
#   consecutively, in the same order.
# - The empty string is a substring of every string: '' in 'abc'.
# - A non-str needle against a str haystack raises TypeError,
#   e.g. 5 in 'abc5'.
# - `in` only answers yes/no. To get a position, use
#   str.find() (returns -1 if absent) or str.index() (raises ValueError).
# - Sets and dicts use hashing, so membership is fast;
#   lists and strings are scanned.
py-easy-59.title: The in operator for membership tests on strings and containers

py-easy-60.syntax:
# General form
#   element in container      -> bool
#   element not in container  -> bool
#
# How `in` is evaluated depends on the container type:
#   - It calls container.__contains__(element) if defined.
#   - Otherwise it falls back to iterating and comparing items.
#
# Example: different containers, same syntax
names = ["ann", "bo", "cy"]
lookup = {"ann", "bo", "cy"}      # set
ages = {"ann": 31, "bo": 27}      # dict (checks keys)

print("bo" in names)      # sequence: compares items one by one
print("bo" in lookup)     # set: uses hashing
print("bo" in ages)       # dict: checks keys, not values

# Gotchas / variations
# - Sequences (list, tuple, str) scan items, comparing with == (or identity).
# - Sets, frozensets, dicts use hash tables; cost is average-case, not worst-case.
# - For repeated lookups on a large list, convert once: s = set(names)
# - Strings test substrings: "an" in "banana" -> True
# - Elements in sets/dict keys must be hashable.
# - Cost of the check also includes the cost of each == comparison.
# - See the Python wiki TimeComplexity page for per-operation costs.
py-easy-60.title: Membership testing with the in operator across containers

py-easy-61.syntax:
# General form
#   set(iterable)   -> new set built from the items of any iterable
#   set()           -> empty set (note: {} makes an empty dict, not a set)
#   {a, b, c}       -> set literal (needs at least one element)

# Examples
letters = set("hello")          # iterates the string's characters
print(len(letters))             # size of the resulting set

names = set(("ann", "bob", "ann"))
print("bob" in names)           # fast membership test -> True

# Key properties
# - A set holds unique, hashable elements; each value is stored once.
# - Sets are unordered: no indexing, and printed order is not guaranteed.
# - Elements must be hashable: set([[1], [2]]) raises TypeError (lists are not).
# - The repr uses curly braces, like a literal, e.g. {'a', 'b'}.
#   An empty set prints as set().
# - Sets are mutable: add(), remove(), discard(), update().
# - frozenset(iterable) is the immutable, hashable variant.
# - Common use: removing duplicates, e.g. list(set(items)) (order may change).
# - Set operations: a | b (union), a & b (intersection), a - b (difference).
# - Literal {1: 1} with key:value pairs is a dict, not a set.
py-easy-61.title: The set() constructor and set literals

py-easy-62.syntax:
# General form: operators combine two sets and return a NEW set
#   a | b    union
#   a & b    intersection
#   a - b    difference
#   a ^ b    symmetric difference

# Example with different values:
x = {10, 20, 30}
y = {30, 40}
print(x | y)   # all elements from either set
print(x - y)   # elements in x but not in y
print(x ^ y)   # elements in exactly one of the sets

# Method forms accept any iterable, not only sets:
x.intersection([20, 30, 99])
x.union(range(3))
x.difference("ab")

# Gotchas:
# - Operators require both sides to be sets (or frozensets);
#   set & list raises TypeError, but set.intersection(list) works.
# - Sets are unordered: printed order may vary.
# - Augmented forms modify in place: a &= b, a |= b, a -= b, a ^= b
# - {} is an empty dict; use set() for an empty set.
# - Result type follows the left operand (set vs frozenset).
py-easy-62.title: Set operators and the equivalent set methods

py-easy-64.syntax:
# General form
#   for key in mapping: ...        # iterates keys
#   mapping.keys() / .values() / .items()   # views over the dict
#
# Example: building and iterating a dict
colors = {}
colors["red"] = 1
colors["blue"] = 2
colors["green"] = 3
for name in colors:
    print(name)

# Example: updating and deleting
colors["red"] = 10      # assigning to an existing key
del colors["blue"]
colors["blue"] = 4      # key added again
print(list(colors))

# Variations and gotchas
# - Language history: CPython 3.6 dicts happened to preserve order as an
#   implementation detail; the language docs define the behavior from a later
#   release. Check the docs' "Changed in version" notes.
# - Views (keys, values, items) reflect the same order as the dict.
# - Changing the value of an existing key does not change its position.
# - Deleting then re-adding a key places it at the end.
# - Equality: dict == dict ignores order; collections.OrderedDict == OrderedDict
#   compares order too.
# - reversed(d) works on dicts (3.8+).
# - Do not add or remove keys while iterating (RuntimeError);
#   iterate over list(d) instead.
# - set does not guarantee insertion order.
py-easy-64.title: Dictionary ordering and iteration

# General form
# s.strip([chars])   -> new string (strings are immutable)
# s.lstrip([chars]) -> removes from the left side only
# s.rstrip([chars]) -> removes from the right side only

# Examples
name = "\t world \n"
name.lstrip()          # removes leading whitespace only
name.rstrip()          # removes trailing whitespace only

path = "xxdataxx"
path.strip("x")        # chars argument: a SET of characters to remove

# Variations and gotchas
# - With no argument, strips all leading AND trailing whitespace
#   (spaces, tabs, newlines, etc.).
# - Whitespace in the middle of the string is never touched.
# - The chars argument is not a prefix/suffix; every listed char is
#   removed from both ends until a non-listed char is reached.
# - The original string is unchanged; you must use the returned value.
# - For removing an exact prefix/suffix use removeprefix()/removesuffix().
# - If nothing is left to keep, the result is the empty string ''.
py-easy-65.title: Trimming whitespace from strings

py-easy-66.syntax:
# General form
#   s.split(sep=None, maxsplit=-1)  -> list of str
#
# Two distinct modes depending on sep:
#   sep=None (or omitted): whitespace mode
#   sep given (e.g. ','):  literal separator mode

# Example 1: explicit separator
row = 'x,,y,z'
print(row.split(','))        # compare each comma: consecutive separators
                             # are handled one by one

# Example 2: default mode on other text
line = '  red\tgreen\n blue  '
print(line.split())          # leading/trailing whitespace is also considered

# Variations and gotchas
# - maxsplit limits the number of splits: s.split(None, 1)
# - With sep=None, whitespace includes space, tab, newline, etc.
# - With a literal sep, every occurrence counts as a boundary,
#   so adjacent separators and separators at the ends matter.
# - ''.split() and '   '.split() in default mode give a list
#   with no items; ''.split(',') gives a list with one item.
# - sep=' ' is NOT the same as sep=None.
# - sep must not be an empty string (ValueError).
# - rsplit() works from the right; splitlines() splits on line breaks.
py-easy-66.title: str.split() separator handling

py-easy-67.syntax:
# General form
#   s.split(sep=None, maxsplit=-1) -> list of str
#
# With an explicit sep, the string is cut at every occurrence of sep.
# The pieces between/around separators become list items, one per cut + 1.

row = "x;y;z"
row.split(";")          # three pieces, one for each field

line = "p|q"
line.split("|", 1)      # maxsplit limits the number of cuts

# Variations and gotchas
# - sep is matched literally (not a regex) and may be multiple characters:
#     "k--v--w".split("--")
# - Adjacent separators, or a separator at the start or end, produce
#   empty strings '' as items (they are NOT skipped) when sep is given.
# - No argument (sep=None) is different: it splits on runs of whitespace
#   and discards empty strings:
#     "  m   n ".split()
# - "".split(",") gives [''] while "".split() gives [].
# - sep="" raises ValueError (empty separator).
# - maxsplit=N gives at most N+1 items; rsplit() counts from the right.
# - To drop empties yourself: [p for p in s.split(",") if p]
py-easy-67.title: str.split with an explicit separator
