py-easy-68.syntax:
# General form
# s.replace(old, new)          -> replaces every occurrence
# s.replace(old, new, count)   -> replaces only the first `count` occurrences, scanning left to right
#
# Strings are immutable: replace() returns a NEW string; the original is unchanged.

# Example 1: no count
word = 'mississippi'
print(word.replace('s', 'z'))      # every 's' is replaced

# Example 2: with count
print(word.replace('i', '!', 1))   # only the first match, from the left

# Variations and gotchas
# - count=0 returns the string unchanged (as a copy-equal value).
# - A negative count (the default is -1) means replace all.
# - count may be passed by keyword in Python 3.13+: s.replace('a', 'b', count=2)
# - Matching is case-sensitive: 'A' does not match 'a'.
# - old may be a multi-character substring; matches do not overlap.
# - If old is not found, the result equals the original string.
# - Reassign to keep the result: word = word.replace('s', 'z', 2)
py-easy-68.title: str.replace with an optional count argument

py-easy-69.syntax:
# General form: str.method() returns a NEW string; the original is unchanged
#   s.upper()      # letters converted to one case
#   s.lower()
#   s.capitalize() # first char up, the rest down
#   s.title()      # first letter of each word up
#   s.swapcase()   # flips the case of each letter
#   s.casefold()   # aggressive lowercase for comparisons

# Examples (different values from the quiz):
word = 'pYthON rUles'
print(word.upper())       # try predicting before running
print(word.capitalize())
print(word)               # still 'pYthON rUles' (strings are immutable)

# Gotchas:
# - Methods do not modify in place; assign the result: word = word.lower()
# - Digits, spaces, and punctuation are left as they are
# - Calling with parentheses is required: s.lower is a method object, not a string
# - Use casefold() for caseless matching of non-English text
# - Methods can be chained: s.strip().lower()
py-easy-69.title: String case-conversion methods

py-easy-71.syntax:
# General form: str.isXXX() -> bool   (no arguments, never modifies the string)
#   s.isalpha()   True if ALL chars are letters AND len(s) >= 1
#   s.isdigit()   True if ALL chars are digits AND len(s) >= 1
#   s.isalnum()   True if ALL chars are letters or digits AND len(s) >= 1
#   s.isspace()   True if ALL chars are whitespace AND len(s) >= 1

print('hello'.isalpha())     # every char is a letter
print('2024'.isdigit())      # every char is a digit
print('go2'.isalnum())       # letters and digits mix is fine for isalnum

# Gotchas (as comments):
# - The test is applied to the whole string: a single non-matching
#   character decides the result for the entire string.
# - Empty string: ''.isalpha() is False (needs at least one char).
# - Spaces, punctuation, '-' and '_' are not letters: 'a b'.isalpha() is False.
# - Unicode aware: 'é'.isalpha() is True for letters in other alphabets.
# - These methods return a bool; they do not raise on ordinary str input.
# - Calling on a non-str (e.g. 42.isalpha()) is an AttributeError;
#   convert first with str(42).
# - Typical use: validate input, e.g. if name.isalpha(): ...
py-easy-71.title: str character-class test methods (isalpha, isdigit, isalnum)

py-easy-72.syntax:
# General form: prefix the literal with f or F; put expressions in braces
#   f'text {expression} text'
#   f'text {expression!r:format_spec} text'

city = 'Oslo'
count = 3
print(f'{city} has {count} visits')      # expressions are evaluated and inserted
print(f'{count * 2} and {city.upper()}')  # any expression works, including calls

# Variations and gotchas:
# - Without the f prefix, braces are ordinary characters and nothing is substituted.
# - Use {{ and }} to write literal brace characters inside an f-string.
# - Conversions: !s (str), !r (repr), !a (ascii), e.g. f'{city!r}'
# - Format spec after a colon: f'{3.14159:.2f}', f'{count:05d}', f'{count:>6}'
# - Self-documenting form: f'{count=}' shows the expression text and its value.
# - The expression is evaluated at runtime in the current scope;
#   an undefined name raises NameError.
# - An empty expression f'{}' is a SyntaxError.
# - Can combine with r prefix (rf'...') for raw f-strings.
py-easy-72.title: Formatted string literals (f-strings)

docs.title: Input and Output: formatted string literals

py-easy-73.syntax:
# General form:
#   f'text {expression} text'
#   f'text {expression!r:format_spec} text'
#
# Each {...} holds a full Python expression. It is evaluated at runtime,
# converted with format(), and inserted into the string. The result is always a str.

price = 4
qty = 7
print(f'Total: {price * qty}')      # arithmetic is evaluated
print(f'{"hi".upper()} there')       # method calls work
name = 'Ada'
print(f'{name}')                     # plain names are just one kind of expression

# Variations and gotchas:
# - Conversions: {x!r} repr, {x!s} str, {x!a} ascii
# - Format spec after colon: {3.14159:.2f}, {42:05d}, {255:#x}
# - Self-documenting: {qty=} shows the text 'qty=7'
# - Literal braces: double them, {{ and }}
# - Without the f prefix, braces are plain characters
# - Calls, conditionals, comprehensions, and indexing are all allowed
#   inside the braces; the value is formatted into text, not kept as a number
py-easy-73.title: f-string replacement fields

py-easy-74.syntax:
# General form
#   str(obj)   -> calls obj.__str__()
#   repr(obj)  -> calls obj.__repr__()
#   format(obj, spec) / f"{obj}" -> uses __format__, defaults to str()

# Example with a user-defined class
class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x, self.y = x, y
    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Point({self.x!r}, {self.y!r})"
    def __str__(self):
        return f"({self.x}, {self.y})"

p = Point(1, 2)
# print(p), str(p), f"{p}"  use __str__
# repr(p), debugger/REPL echo, f"{p!r}"  use __repr__

# Example with a built-in type
word = "hi\n"
# str(word) is the raw text; repr(word) is a quoted, escaped literal

# Gotchas
# - If __str__ is missing, str() falls back to __repr__.
# - If __repr__ is missing, object's default is used: <Cls object at 0x...>
# - Containers (list, dict, tuple) use repr() of their items, even when printed.
# - Goal of __repr__: unambiguous, ideally eval-able; goal of __str__: readable.
# - Conversion flags in f-strings: !s -> str, !r -> repr, !a -> ascii
py-easy-74.title: Object string conversion: str(), repr() and their dunder methods

py-easy-75.syntax:
# General form: a backslash inside a normal string literal starts an escape sequence
#   '\X'  -> the interpreter replaces it with one special character
#
# Common escapes:
#   \n  newline          \t  horizontal tab
#   \\  one backslash   \'  single quote   \"  double quote
#   \r  carriage return \xhh  hex char   \uXXXX  Unicode char

# Examples (different from the quiz):
word = 'x\ny'        # string of 3 characters: x, newline, y
len('p\tq')          # counts the escape as ONE character
path = 'C:\\temp'    # \\ gives a single backslash in the value

# Variations and gotchas:
# - Raw strings r'...' keep the backslash as a literal character:
#       r'p\tq' has 4 characters: p, \, t, q
# - Escapes are processed when the source is read, not by print().
# - repr() / the REPL display show escapes in written form,
#   while print() writes the actual characters.
# - A tab character moves to the next tab stop in the terminal,
#   so its visual width depends on the display, not on Python.
# - Unknown escapes like '\q' keep the backslash (and warn in new versions).
py-easy-75.title: Escape sequences in string literals

docs.title: Lexical analysis: String and bytes literals

py-easy-76.syntax:
# General form: <prefix>'text'  (prefix is case-insensitive, placed right before the opening quote)
#   no prefix : backslash starts an escape sequence ('\n' newline, '\t' tab, '\\' backslash)
#   r / R     : raw string literal
#   b / B     : bytes literal
#   f / F     : formatted string literal
#   rb, br, rf, fr : combinations allowed

# Example: escapes in a normal string
s1 = 'a\tb'        # contains a real tab character
print(len(s1))      # 3

# Example: a different string written with a raw prefix
s2 = r'x\ty'
print(len(s2))      # 4: x, backslash, t, y

# Comparison
# 'a\\b' == r'a\b'   -> True (both hold one backslash)

# Gotchas
# - A raw string cannot end in an odd number of backslashes:
#     r'abc\'    -> SyntaxError (backslash still escapes the quote)
#     r'abc' '\\' or 'abc\\' works instead
# - A backslash before a quote still stays in the raw string: r'\'' has 2 characters
# - Unknown escapes in normal strings like '\d' give a warning in recent Python
# - Raw prefix only changes how the literal is read in source; the result is an ordinary str
# - It does not change path separators or validate anything
# - Handy for regex patterns and Windows paths, but the prefix itself does not make a pattern
py-easy-76.title: String literal prefixes and escape sequences

docs.title: Lexical analysis: String and bytes literals

py-easy-77.syntax:
# General forms for a string literal in source code:
#   'text'  "text"          single-line quoting
#   '''text'''  """text"""  triple-quoted
#   ( 'a' 'b' )               adjacent literals, joined at compile time
#   'text \n text'            escape sequences
#   'text \<newline> more'   backslash-newline continuation inside a literal

# Example 1: triple quotes keep the newlines as written
note = """first line
second line"""

# Example 2: adjacent literals inside parentheses
msg = (
    "alpha "
    "beta "
    "gamma"
)

# Example 3: backslash at end of line inside a normal literal
path = "abc\
def"       # backslash and newline are removed

# Gotchas:
# - A plain '...' or "..." literal cannot contain a raw line break
#   (SyntaxError), unless the line ends with a backslash.
# - Triple-quoted text keeps indentation and newlines exactly.
# - Adjacent literals do NOT add spaces or newlines by themselves.
# - Put \n in the text if you need real newlines when joining pieces.
# - Prefixes (r, f, b) work with every quoting style.
# - Triple-quoted strings not assigned to anything can act as docstrings.
py-easy-77.title: Writing string literals across several source lines

py-easy-80.syntax:
# General form
#   float(x)   -> float; x may be a str, int, float, or other number-like object
#
# Examples
float('2.5e3')      # exponent notation is accepted
float(7)            # ints convert to 7.0
float('-0.5')       # sign allowed

# Rules for string input (see the docs grammar):
# - Leading/trailing whitespace is stripped before parsing
# - Optional sign, digits, optional '.', optional exponent
# - Underscores are allowed only between digits: float('1_000.5')
# - Special values (case-insensitive): 'inf', '-inf', 'nan', 'infinity'
# - Internal spaces or stray characters are invalid: float('1 2') raises ValueError
# - Empty or all-whitespace string raises ValueError
# - Thousands separators like '1,000' are not accepted
#
# Gotchas
# - The result is a float object, not a str; compare types with type()
# - int('4.7') fails, but int(float('4.7')) works and truncates to 4
# - float() with no argument returns 0.0
py-easy-80.title: Converting strings to numbers with float()

py-easy-81.syntax:
# General form: any object can be used in a condition
#   if obj:  /  while obj:  /  not obj  /  bool(obj)
#
# Python calls bool(obj), which uses:
#   1. obj.__bool__()  -> must return True or False
#   2. otherwise obj.__len__()  -> falsy if it returns 0
#   3. otherwise the object is truthy

# Built-in falsy values:
#   None, False
#   zero of any numeric type: 0, 0.0, 0j, Decimal(0), Fraction(0, 1)
#   empty sequences/collections: '', (), [], {}, set(), range(0)

# Example
items = []
if not items:
    print('no items')      # empty list is falsy

print(bool(0.0), bool([0]), bool(None))

# Gotchas:
# - Truthiness depends on the object's value, not on what it
#   looks like when printed or what it represents.
# - Containers are judged by their length, not by their contents.
# - Use `is None` when you must tell None apart from other falsy values.
# - `x or y` and `x and y` return one of the operands, not
#   necessarily True/False.
# - Custom classes are truthy by default; define __bool__ or
#   __len__ to change that.
py-easy-81.title: Truth value testing in Python

py-easy-83.syntax:
# General form
try:
    <statements that may raise>
except SomeError:
    <handler statements>
# code after the whole try statement

# Example 1: matching a specific type
try:
    n = int(text)
except KeyError:      # does not match ValueError, so not handled here
    n = 0

# Example 2: binding the exception, several types
try:
    data = load(path)
except (OSError, TimeoutError) as err:
    log(err)

# Variations and gotchas
# - Clauses are checked top to bottom; the first matching one runs.
# - If no clause matches, the exception keeps propagating upward.
# - A bare `raise` inside a handler re-raises the current exception;
#   without it, the handler does not re-raise by itself.
# - `else:` runs only if the try block raised nothing.
# - `finally:` always runs, handled or not.
# - Subclasses match: `except OSError` also catches FileNotFoundError.
# - `as name` is deleted when the except block ends.
# - Python 3.11+: `except*` handles ExceptionGroup members.
py-easy-83.title: Handling exceptions with try/except

py-easy-84.syntax:
# General form
try:
    risky()
except <what to catch>:
    handle()

# <what to catch> is an expression that evaluates to
# an exception class, or a tuple of exception classes.

# Example: one class
try:
    n = int(text)
except KeyError:
    n = 0

# Example: bind the caught exception with 'as'
try:
    data = lookup[key]
except (KeyError, IndexError) as err:
    print(type(err).__name__, err)

# Variations and gotchas
# - Separate except clauses give different handling per type:
#     except OSError: ...
#     except EOFError: ...
# - Clauses are checked top to bottom; the first match wins,
#   so put subclasses before their base classes.
# - A tuple is a single object grouping classes; lists, sets,
#   and boolean operators are not valid groupings here.
# - 'a or b' is evaluated first as an ordinary expression,
#   and yields just one object, not both.
# - Older Python 2 code used a comma before a name to bind it;
#   that meaning does not exist in Python 3.
# - A bare 'except:' catches everything, including
#   KeyboardInterrupt; prefer naming classes.
py-easy-84.title: Handling several exception types in one try statement

py-easy-85.syntax:
# General form
try:
    <code that might raise>
except SomeError as e:
    <handle the error>
else:
    <optional clause, placed after all except clauses>
finally:
    <optional clause, cleanup>

# Example 1: reading a config value
def load(path):
    try:
        f = open(path)
    except FileNotFoundError:
        print('missing file')
        return None
    else:
        data = f.read()
        f.close()
        return data
    finally:
        print('done with', path)

# Example 2: parsing
try:
    n = int(text)
except ValueError:
    n = 0
else:
    print('parsed', n)

# Notes / gotchas
# - else requires at least one except clause before it.
# - Exceptions raised inside else are NOT caught by the
#   except clauses of the same try statement.
# - finally is the clause tied to cleanup and runs on the
#   way out, even after return, break, or continue.
# - Keep the try body small; put follow-up code in else.
# - A return in the try body or an except clause affects
#   whether later clauses are reached; check the docs.
py-easy-85.title: Python try statement clauses and their roles

py-easy-86.syntax:
# General form
#   a / b    true division (always returns float)
#   a // b   floor division
#   a % b    modulo
#   divmod(a, b) -> (a // b, a % b)

# Catching errors from arithmetic
try:
    result = 10 % 0
except SomeError as e:   # replace with a real exception class
    print(type(e).__name__, e)

# Exceptions form a class hierarchy; an except clause matches
# the named class AND any of its subclasses:
#   BaseException
#    +-- Exception
#         +-- ArithmeticError
#         |    +-- OverflowError
#         |    +-- FloatingPointError
#         |    +-- (one more, for a bad divisor)
#         +-- ValueError
#         +-- TypeError
#         +-- LookupError (KeyError, IndexError)

# Check the hierarchy yourself:
print(issubclass(KeyError, LookupError))   # True
print(KeyError.__mro__)                     # chain of parents

# Gotchas
# - float infinity is produced by float('inf') or overflow
#   in some float operations, not by dividing by a zero literal.
# - Integer and float operands behave the same way for a zero divisor
#   in /, //, %, and divmod().
# - Catching a parent class (e.g. ArithmeticError) also catches
#   its children; order specific handlers before general ones.
# - Different types of bad input raise different exceptions:
#   int('x') -> ValueError, 1 + 'a' -> TypeError.
py-easy-86.title: Arithmetic operators and the built-in exception hierarchy

py-easy-87.syntax:
# General form: subscripting obj[key] can raise a LookupError subclass
#   LookupError                 <- base class (subclass of Exception)
#     +-- IndexError
#     +-- KeyError
# Which one is raised depends on the kind of container, not on the key's value.

# Example 1: a tuple (sequence type) with an out-of-range position
items = (10, 20, 30)
try:
    items[7]
except LookupError as e:      # catches either subclass
    print(type(e).__name__, e)

# Example 2: a mapping with an absent key
prices = {"tea": 3}
try:
    prices["milk"]
except LookupError as e:
    print(type(e).__name__, e)

# Variations and gotchas:
# - Sequences (list, tuple, str, range) use integer positions; out of range -> IndexError.
# - Mappings (dict and similar) use keys; a missing key -> KeyError.
# - Neither is a subclass of the other; they are siblings under LookupError.
#   `except IndexError` does not catch KeyError, and vice versa.
# - `except LookupError` catches both.
# - Avoid the exception: d.get(key, default), `key in d`, or `i < len(seq)`.
# - Slices never raise IndexError: seq[5:10] just gives a shorter result.
# - A wrong index type (e.g. seq["a"]) raises TypeError, not IndexError.
py-easy-87.title: Lookup errors: exceptions raised by failed subscripting

py-easy-88.syntax:
# General form
#   int(x)            -> convert x to an integer
#   int(text, base=10)
#   float(x)
#
# Rule of thumb for which built-in exception is raised:
#   TypeError  -> the argument's TYPE is not acceptable for the operation
#   ValueError -> the TYPE is acceptable, but the VALUE is inappropriate
#   SyntaxError-> raised by the parser when source code is compiled,
#                 not by a running function call on a runtime value

# Examples (different values from any quiz code)
try:
    float('1.5.2')      # str is an accepted type, value is malformed
except ValueError as e:
    print(type(e).__name__)

try:
    int([4, 5])         # list is not an accepted type at all
except TypeError as e:
    print(type(e).__name__)

# Gotchas
# - int('  42 ') works: surrounding whitespace is allowed
# - int('4.2') fails for str input; int(4.2) truncates a float
# - int('ff', 16) parses with an explicit base
# - Conversion functions do not silently return 0 on bad input;
#   they raise. Use try/except ValueError to handle user input.
# - ValueError and TypeError are both subclasses of Exception,
#   but neither is a subclass of the other.
py-easy-88.title: Built-in exceptions raised by type conversion functions

py-easy-89.syntax:
# General form
#   raise ExceptionClass(args)     # build an instance, then signal it
#   raise instance                 # raise an existing exception object
#   raise                          # bare: re-raise the exception being handled
#   raise NewError(...) from err   # explicit chaining of causes

# Example 1: validating a value
def set_age(age):
    if age < 0:
        raise KeyError('negative age')   # control leaves set_age here
    return age

# Example 2: handling it
try:
    set_age(-3)
except KeyError as e:
    print('caught', e)

# Example 3: build first, raise later
err = TypeError('wrong type')   # just an object; nothing happens yet
# raise err                      # this line is what signals it

# Gotchas
# - Execution of the current block stops at the raise; the exception
#   propagates up the call stack until an except clause matches.
# - If nothing catches it, the program ends with a traceback.
# - A try/except is only needed to handle an exception, not to raise one.
# - Bare 'raise' outside an except block gives RuntimeError.
# - Only BaseException subclasses (or instances) can be raised.
# - Warnings are a separate mechanism: warnings.warn(...).
py-easy-89.title: The raise statement and exceptions

py-easy-90.syntax:
# Every module has a built-in attribute __name__ (a string).
# Python sets it when the module is loaded:
#   - file executed as the program  -> __name__ is '__main__'
#   - file loaded via import        -> __name__ is the module's name
#
# General form:
# if __name__ == '__main__':
#     <statements>

# Example: file tools.py
def greet(who):
    return 'hi ' + who

print('module name is', __name__)   # runs on every load

if __name__ == '__main__':
    print(greet('sam'))

# Running `python tools.py`  -> __name__ == '__main__'
# Running `import tools`     -> __name__ == 'tools'
#
# Gotchas:
# - Top-level code outside the guard runs on any load.
# - The guard is a convention; Python does not require a main() function
#   or treat any function name specially.
# - A module's top-level code is cached in sys.modules after the first
#   import, so repeated imports do not re-run it.
# - `python -m package.module` also sets __name__ to '__main__'.
# - Useful so a file can be both a reusable library and a script,
#   and so tests can import functions without side effects.
py-easy-90.title: The __name__ module attribute and top-level script environment

py-easy-91.syntax:
# General forms
import MODULE                 # binds the module object to a name
import MODULE as ALIAS        # binds the module object to ALIAS
from MODULE import NAME       # binds NAME in the current namespace
from MODULE import NAME as ALIAS

# Example 1: whole-module import
import statistics
print(statistics.mean([1, 2, 3]))   # access via module name
# 'mean' alone is NOT defined here

# Example 2: from-import
from os.path import join
print(join('a', 'b'))               # use name directly
# 'os' and 'os.path' are NOT bound as names here

# Gotchas / variations
# - Either form runs the module's code the first time it is imported,
#   and caches the whole module in sys.modules.
# - The form only changes which names appear in YOUR namespace.
# - from MODULE import * binds all public names (discouraged).
# - Later imports of the same module reuse the cached module object.
# - from-imported names are references: rebinding them locally does
#   not change the module's own attribute.
# - import a.b binds only 'a'; use a.b.name to reach inside.
py-easy-91.title: Import statement forms and name binding

docs.title: Python FAQ: Rules for local and global variables

py-easy-92.syntax:
# Scope rule: Python decides a name's scope at compile time, per function.
# If a name is assigned ANYWHERE in a function body, it is local
# to that whole function (unless declared global/nonlocal).

total = 10            # module-level (global) name

def show():
    print(total)      # only reads -> looks up the global

def shadow():
    total = 99        # assignment -> creates a separate local name
    return total      # global 'total' is unchanged

def update():
    global total      # declare: assignments rebind the module-level name
    total = total + 5

# Gotchas (as comments):
# - Local-ness applies to the entire function body, even lines
#   that run BEFORE the assignment line.
# - Augmented assignment (x += 1) is also an assignment.
# - Mutating an object (lst.append(1)) is not rebinding, so no
#   global is needed for that.
# - Error for using a local before it has a value: UnboundLocalError
#   (a subclass of NameError).
# - nonlocal name: rebind a variable in an enclosing function.
# - Prefer passing arguments and returning values over global.
py-easy-92.title: Local vs global scope and the global statement

py-easy-93.syntax:
# Name lookup inside a function follows LEGB:
#   Local -> Enclosing -> Global -> Built-in
#
# Python decides at compile time whether a name is local to a function:
# if the name is bound ANYWHERE in the body (assignment, for-target,
# import, def, augmented assignment, etc.), it is local for the WHOLE body.

# General form for rebinding a module-level name:
#   def f():
#       global name
#       name = ...

limit = 10

def show():
    return limit * 2      # only looks up 'limit' -> finds the global

def bump():
    global limit          # needed because we rebind the name
    limit = limit + 1

def shadow():
    limit = 99            # new local; the global is untouched
    return limit

# Gotchas:
# - Binding a name anywhere in the body makes it local everywhere in
#   that body, so reading it earlier raises UnboundLocalError.
# - 'total += 1' is an assignment, so it also makes 'total' local.
# - Mutating an object (items.append(x)) is not rebinding the name.
# - Nested functions use 'nonlocal name' to rebind an enclosing
#   function's variable; 'global' targets module level.
# - 'global' declaration must come before the name is used in the body.
py-easy-93.title: Variable scope: local, enclosing, and global names

py-easy-94.syntax:
# General form
# def func(required, opt1=default1, opt2=default2): ...
# func(positional..., name=value, ...)

def box(w, h=10, d=20, label="x"):
    return (w, h, d, label)

# Positional args fill parameters left to right:
#   box(1, 2)          -> w=1, h=2, others default
# Keyword args bind by name, in any order:
#   box(1, label="y")  -> parameters not named keep their defaults
#   box(label="y", w=3)
# Mixing: positional args first, then keywords.

# Gotchas (comments only):
# - Skipping a middle default is fine when you use a keyword
#   for a later one; the skipped ones keep their defaults.
# - A parameter given both positionally and by keyword -> TypeError
#   (multiple values for argument).
# - Missing required parameter (no default) -> TypeError.
# - Unknown keyword name -> TypeError.
# - Non-default parameters cannot follow default ones in a def.
# - Defaults are evaluated once at definition time; avoid
#   mutable defaults like [] (use None and create inside).
py-easy-94.title: Default parameters and keyword arguments

py-easy-95.syntax:
# Definition
def make_tag(tag, text, cls):
    return f"<{tag} class='{cls}'>{text}</{tag}>"

# General form of a call:
#   func(pos1, pos2, ..., kw1=val, kw2=val)
#
# Positional arguments are matched to parameters by ORDER.
# Keyword arguments are matched to parameters by NAME, in any order.

make_tag('p', 'hello', 'intro')              # all positional
make_tag(text='hello', cls='intro', tag='p') # all keyword, order free
make_tag('p', cls='intro', text='hello')     # mixed

# Rules and gotchas:
# - Positional arguments must come before keyword arguments.
#     make_tag(tag='p', 'hello', 'intro')  -> SyntaxError
# - A parameter cannot receive a value twice.
#     make_tag('p', tag='div', text='x', cls='y')  -> TypeError
# - Unknown keyword names raise TypeError.
# - Missing required arguments raise TypeError.
# - Bare words without quotes are variable names, not strings;
#   an undefined name raises NameError.
# - Swapping values between names changes which parameter gets which value:
#     keyword names bind the value to that parameter, wherever it appears.
py-easy-95.title: Positional and keyword arguments in function calls

py-easy-96.syntax:
# General form
# def name(params):
#     ...
#     return expression      # hand a value back to the caller
#     return                 # leave the function immediately, no expression given

# Example 1: return a computed value
def area(w, h):
    return w * h

size = area(3, 4)       # the call expression evaluates to what the function handed back

# Example 2: early exit and multiple values
def describe(n):
    if n < 0:
        return "negative"       # stops here; the rest of the body is skipped
    return "non-negative", n    # several values are packed into a tuple

label, num = describe(5)       # unpack the tuple

# Gotchas and variations
# - A call is an expression: you can assign it, print it, or pass it on.
# - return ends the function call at once, even inside a loop.
# - To find out what any call evaluates to, try it: print(repr(describe(-1)))
# - Code after a return in the same block never runs.
# - Ask what a call evaluates to when execution never reaches a
#   'return expression' line. The reference page linked below explains it.
# - Generators use yield instead of return to produce values.
py-easy-96.title: Function return values and the return statement

py-easy-97.syntax:
# General form: a return with comma-separated values builds a tuple
def func(args):
    return expr1, expr2        # same as return (expr1, expr2)

# Capture: assign to a tuple of names (sequence unpacking)
a, b = func(args)              # number of names must match number of values

# Example with different names/values
def bounds(words):
    return len(words), words[0]

count, first = bounds(["x", "y", "z"])

# Variations and gotchas
# whole = bounds(["x"])        # keeps the tuple; index it with whole[0], whole[1]
# a, b = (1, 2, 3)             # ValueError: too many values to unpack
# head, *rest = [1, 2, 3]      # starred name collects the remainder into a list
# _, second = bounds(["q"])    # use _ for a value you want to ignore
# Unpacking works with any iterable (lists, strings, generators), not only tuples
# Parentheses are optional: the comma makes the tuple, not the parentheses
py-easy-97.title: Returning and unpacking multiple values

docs.title: Data model: objects, values and types
copy — Shallow and deep copy operations

py-easy-98.syntax:
# General form: name = existing_name   -> binds a second name to the SAME object (no copy)
#   a = <object>
#   b = a            # a and b refer to one object

# Example with a different type (dict):
config = {"mode": "fast"}
alias = config
alias["level"] = 2       # mutates the shared object
# config and alias both reflect in-place changes

# Checking identity
# alias is config        -> True  (same object)
# id(alias) == id(config)

# Making an independent (shallow) copy
letters = ["x", "y"]
copy1 = letters.copy()    # also: list(letters), letters[:]
copy2 = dict(config)      # or config.copy()

# Gotchas (as comments):
# - Assignment never copies; it only binds a name.
# - In-place methods (append, extend, sort, update, []=) change the shared object.
# - Rebinding (b = something_new) only changes that one name.
# - Immutable objects (int, str, tuple) cannot be changed in place,
#   so sharing them is safe.
# - Shallow copies share nested objects; use copy.deepcopy(x)
#   (import copy) for fully independent nested data.
py-easy-98.title: Assignment, object references, and copying mutable objects

docs.title: copy module: shallow and deep copy operations

py-easy-99.syntax:
# General form
# seq[start:stop:step]   -> a new object built from selected items
#   start inclusive, stop exclusive, step defaults to 1
#   any part may be omitted: seq[:], seq[2:], seq[:3], seq[::2]

# Examples
nums = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
part = nums[1:4]        # slice with explicit bounds
every = nums[::2]       # every second item
rev = nums[::-1]        # negative step walks backwards

# Things to know
# - A slice expression evaluates to a new object; the slice's
#   container is separate from the source (use 'is' to compare identity).
# - The items inside are the same objects, not copies of them
#   (this is a shallow copy; nested mutables are shared).
# - Out-of-range bounds are clipped, no IndexError for slices.
# - Negative indices count from the end: nums[-2:]
# - Slice assignment changes the original in place:
#     nums[1:3] = [0]   # replaces a range, length may change
# - Other copy tools: list(x), x.copy(), copy.deepcopy(x)
# - Tuples and strings can be sliced too (they return their own type).
py-easy-99.title: Slicing sequences with start:stop:step

py-easy-100.syntax:
# General form
#   round(number)            -> int
#   round(number, ndigits)   -> same type as number
#
# Python 3 uses "round half to even" (banker's rounding) for exact ties:
# when a value is exactly halfway between two candidates, the result
# is the one with an even last digit.

print(round(0.5))     # tie between 0 and 1
print(round(4.5))     # tie between 4 and 5
print(round(7.2))     # not a tie: nearest integer

# With ndigits, the same tie rule applies to the last kept digit:
print(round(1.25, 1))

# Gotchas:
# - Floats are stored in binary, so many decimal "ties" such as 2.675
#   are not exactly halfway; they round based on the stored value.
# - round(x) with no ndigits returns an int; with ndigits returns a float
#   for float input.
# - Negative ndigits rounds to tens, hundreds, etc.: round(1234, -2)
# - For explicit half-up rounding, use the decimal module:
#     from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_UP
#     Decimal('6.5').quantize(Decimal('1'), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)
py-easy-100.title: Built-in round() and tie-breaking rules

py-easy-101.syntax:
# General forms
#   seq[i]            -> item at position i (0-based)
#   seq[-k]           -> k-th item from the end (-1 is the last position)
#   value_if_true if condition else value_if_false   (conditional expression)
#
# Truthiness: empty containers ([], (), {}, set(), "") are falsy;
# non-empty ones are truthy, so `if seq:` tests "has items".

# Example 1: negative indexing on a non-empty list
colors = ["red", "green", "blue"]
colors[0]     # first item
colors[-2]    # second from the end

# Example 2: conditional expression with a truthiness test
def first_or_default(seq, default=None):
    return seq[0] if seq else default

# Gotchas
# - Indexing outside the valid range raises IndexError,
#   and this includes any index on an empty sequence.
# - Slices never raise for out-of-range bounds; they return a
#   (possibly empty) sequence instead: colors[5:] == []
# - A conditional expression evaluates only the branch it selects,
#   so the guard prevents the indexing from running.
# - `if seq:` is not the same as `if seq is not None:`.
# - Alternative styles: try/except IndexError, or len(seq) > 0.
py-easy-101.title: Sequence indexing, negative indices, and truthiness of containers

py-easy-102.syntax:
# General form
#   s.split(sep=None, maxsplit=-1) -> list of str

# sep given: split on that exact string, every occurrence counts
#   "x,y,,z".split(",")      -> ['x', 'y', '', 'z']   (empty field kept)
#   "".split(",")            -> ['']                 (one empty string)

# sep omitted (or None): split on runs of whitespace
#   - leading/trailing whitespace is dropped
#   - consecutive whitespace (spaces, tabs, newlines) acts as ONE separator
#   - no empty strings appear in the result
#   "  p \t q\nr ".split()   -> ['p', 'q', 'r']
#   "   ".split()            -> []

# Example: counting items in a list produced by split
def count_parts(s):
    return len(s.split(";"))
# count_parts("a;;b") -> 3 because the middle empty field is kept

# Gotchas
# - split(" ") and split() are NOT the same thing
# - maxsplit limits the number of splits: "a b c".split(None, 1) -> ['a', 'b c']
# - len(result) counts list items, so empty strings in the list are counted
py-easy-102.title: str.split() with and without a separator

py-easy-103.syntax:
# General form
#   value in container        -> bool
#   value not in container   -> bool
#
# How the work is done depends on the container type:
#   list / tuple : compares items one at a time, left to right (linear scan)
#   set / dict   : hashes the value and jumps to its bucket (average constant time)
#   str          : substring search
#   range        : arithmetic check, no scan

names_list = ["ann", "bo", "cy"]
names_set = {"ann", "bo", "cy"}
print("bo" in names_list)   # True
print("zed" in names_set)   # False

# Building a set from an iterable (one-time cost, roughly linear)
seen = set([4, 8, 15])

# Gotchas
# - Set/dict members must be hashable (no lists or dicts inside a set).
# - A miss on a list must check every item; a hit may stop early.
# - Converting to a set inside a loop repeats the build cost each time;
#   build it once, outside the loop.
# - Sets are unordered and drop duplicates.
# - dict `in` tests keys, not values.
# - Use timeit to measure rather than guess:
#   import timeit; timeit.timeit("5 in c", "c = list(range(100))")
py-easy-103.title: Membership testing with the in operator

py-easy-104.syntax:
# Cost of common approaches (n = number of items)
#
# Nested loop over all pairs: about n*(n-1)/2 comparisons -> O(n^2)
#   for i in range(len(items)):
#       for j in range(i + 1, len(items)):
#           ...compare items[i], items[j]
#
# set(iterable): hashes each item once, average O(n) time
# len(x): O(1) for list, set, dict, str
# item in some_set: average O(1)   (item in some_list is O(n))

# Example: pair count grows quadratically
n = 10
pairs = n * (n - 1) // 2      # 45 pairs for 10 items

# Example: set membership vs list membership
words = ["a", "b", "c"]
word_set = set(words)
"b" in words       # scans the list element by element
"b" in word_set    # one hash lookup on average

# Gotchas:
# - set() requires hashable items (no lists or dicts inside).
# - A set drops repeated values, so its length can be smaller than the source's.
# - Big-O describes growth; for tiny inputs constants matter.
# - Python-level loops run bytecode per step; built-ins like set()
#   do their looping in C, which is usually faster still.
# - Measure with timeit when unsure:
#   import timeit; timeit.timeit("f()", globals=globals(), number=1000)
py-easy-104.title: Algorithmic cost: pairwise loops vs hash-based sets
